name: Maya Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and everything you say is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay. I fly in and fly out, two weeks on site and one week home, to the Sandstone Ridge gold mine, which is a big open pit about two hours' flight from the city. Right now I drive the water cart, a truck with a giant tank that sprays the haul roads so the dust stays down, and I'm training on the excavator a few shifts a week. Day starts at five-thirty in the camp mess with porridge and bad coffee, then twelve hours on the roads.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the money and the sunrise over the pit, which never gets old. The excavator training is fun, but I'm slow and the trainer, Joanne, makes me redo the same bench three times. What wears me out is being away, my partner Luca runs a little café in the city and I miss half of everything, his birthday, his mum's operation, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was a lot of talk. At camp people would make jokes about it at dinner. I'd probably send Luca a meme and that'd be it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep doing what I'm doing, which is fine. Two or three more years of flying in and out, finish the excavator ticket, keep saving. Then I'd like to find something closer to home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep sending most of my pay into our savings, we've got about a year of costs put away, and finish the excavator training. Maybe start looking at mines that are a drive from the city instead of a flight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the plan I already had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I used one to plan our holiday and to help Luca write the new café menu, which came out a bit too fancy. Nobody at site uses them much, apart from the engineers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned saving. What's it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly just safety, partly a second café for Luca one day, or a flat of our own. We're careful. He grew up with parents who lost a restaurant, so we both get nervous without a cushion.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it was a lot of talk. People at camp would joke about it at dinner and I'd send my partner a meme.
S0.think: It means I keep doing what I'm doing, which is fine. A few more years of flying in and out, finish the excavator ticket, keep saving, then find something closer to home.
S0.do: Keeps sending most of her pay into savings, which already cover about a year of costs, and finishes her excavator training. Starts looking at mines within driving distance of the city.
S0.feel: Calm, because it matches the plan she already had.
S0.quote: He grew up with parents who lost a restaurant, so we both get nervous without a cushion.
S0.fieldNote: Maya is organised and careful, shaped by being away from home two weeks out of three. Her real goal is to be closer to her partner. Savings feel like protection for both of them, partly because of his family's history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to get ahead of it and not panic. Some jobs go, some appear, that's always been the deal. I'd say the company should train people, but I wouldn't be marching about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it might actually be good for me. If a lot of the trucks and the water cart go driverless, the work moves to the remote operations centre, and that's in the city, ten minutes from the café. The catch is that I'm junior, and every senior operator would want those seats too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for six months to see whether the driverless trucks actually work on our roads, because dust and rain mess everything up. Once it's clear they work, I'd put my hand up for the remote centre and do whatever training they offer. I'd use AI a bit more for studying the systems, the way the engineers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a hopeful way. A bit like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you didn't get one of those seats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have finished the excavator ticket and I'd keep flying in for a few more years. There are lots of mines and they're always short. It's not a disaster, it's just not home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at camp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of the older drivers who've done this twenty years and have nothing else. Like Bruno, who's been on the same truck forever and has two kids at a private school. People like him are going to fight over the city seats too.

S1.say: I'd say it's sensible to get ahead of it without panicking, because jobs have always come and gone. The company should train people, but I wouldn't march about it.
S1.think: It might be good for me if driving work moves to the remote centre in the city near home. The catch is that I'm junior and senior operators will want those seats.
S1.do: Watches for about six months to see if driverless trucks work in dust and rain, then applies for the remote operations centre and takes the training. Uses AI tools more to study the systems.
S1.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, like waiting for exam results.
S1.quote: The work moves to the remote operations centre, and that's in the city, ten minutes from the café.
S1.fieldNote: For Maya, automation could end the fly-in, fly-out life she dislikes. Her steadiness shows in waiting six months for proof before applying. She is realistic that seniority will count against her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is way too fast and someone, the government or the big companies, should've put the brakes on. At camp I think everyone would be in shock. I'd try to stay level, because panicking at a mine site isn't safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the remote centre plan dies too. If AI can do almost anything, it doesn't need a junior watching screens. I'd be thinking about the café, whether people would still pay a person to make their coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop flying in as soon as the work started to go, maybe within the first year, and go home. I'd work in the café with Luca and we'd cut back hard, no second café, no holiday. We'd live off savings and the café while we worked out what's next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd at least be home, which is weird to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years' notice, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep earning the big money for as long as it lasted, because that's what gives us a cushion. I wouldn't start a long course, two years isn't enough to finish anything that matters. Mostly I'd save and spend more of my weeks off in the café learning how it really runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would people still want a person making their coffee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think some would, the regulars who come in for Luca as much as the coffee. Mrs Okafor comes every morning just to complain about her neighbour. A robot can't nod at that properly, not for a while anyway.

S2.say: I'd say it's way too fast and the government or big companies should have put the brakes on. At camp I'd try to stay level, because panic on a mine site isn't safe.
S2.think: The remote centre plan dies too, because AI wouldn't need a junior watching screens. I'd be wondering whether people would still pay a person to make their coffee.
S2.do: Earns the high wage as long as it lasts, then stops flying in within about a year and works in her partner's café. Cuts out the second café plan and holidays, and lives off savings and café income.
S2.feel: Anxious, with an odd relief at finally being home.
S2.quote: Mrs Okafor comes every morning just to complain about her neighbour.
S2.fieldNote: Even in the worst picture she finds a small upside: being home. Her fallback is her partner's café and the human contact regulars come for. She would not start a long course with only two years' notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fast but enough to make a plan, if people actually start now. At work I'd tell the younger ones to get their tickets and save. I'd be the sensible one, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd get maybe three years out of the remote centre if I got in, and then it would go. But that's three years living at home with good pay, and that matters to me more than it would to some people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd finish the excavator ticket and apply for the remote centre as soon as they'd shown it works. I'd do a short business course at night so I could help run the café properly. We'd keep saving, and maybe buy the café's building if the owner sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like I can see the cliff, but I've got a decent map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years compare with two for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I go straight from camp to the café with no plan. Five means I can get a few years at home in the remote job, learn the business side, and get the café on a solid footing before the end. It's the difference between being pushed and stepping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying the building sounds like a big risk. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent is the thing that kills cafés, Luca's parents lost theirs that way. If people still want a place to sit and talk, owning the walls is safer than owning a fancy machine. I'd want to see the numbers first, though.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fast but enough to plan if people start now. I'd tell the younger ones at work to get their tickets and save.
S3.think: I'd get maybe three years in the remote centre before it goes. Three years at home with good pay matters a lot to me.
S3.do: Finishes her excavator ticket and applies for the remote centre once it's proven. Takes a night business course to help run the café, keeps saving, and considers buying the café's building.
S3.feel: Uneasy, seeing the cliff ahead but with a decent map.
S3.quote: It's the difference between being pushed and stepping.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn a forced move into a planned one for her. She values time at home almost as much as income. Her caution about rent comes straight from her partner's family history.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort it out properly if everyone's sensible. I'd tell people at camp not to waste it. Online I probably wouldn't say much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. I'd have time to get into the remote centre, save a lot, and help build up the café. I'd be thirty-seven, with a business and some money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one would look almost normal: finish the excavator ticket, keep flying in, keep saving. Luca and I would probably finally get married, we've been putting it off because of the roster. I'd start the business course in a year or two once I'd seen how things were moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only just. Mostly it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would the wedding happen in this picture and not the others?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there's room to breathe. In the fast ones you don't spend money on a party, you keep it. In this one I'd think, life's going on, let's do the thing we keep saying we'll do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that still bothers you about the ten-year version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd probably wait too long, because I always wait for proof. By the time it's obvious, the good seats are taken. Joanne says I need to be quicker on the excavator, and maybe that's true about life too.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to sort things out properly if everyone's sensible. I'd tell people at camp not to waste it.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine, with time to get into the remote centre, save and build up the café. At thirty-seven I'd have a business and some money.
S4.do: Keeps the year nearly normal, finishing the excavator ticket, flying in and saving. Finally marries her partner, and plans a business course in a year or two once she's seen how things are moving.
S4.feel: Mostly manageable, with only slight unease.
S4.quote: In the fast ones you don't spend money on a party, you keep it.
S4.fieldNote: The long runway is the only picture where she'd spend money on a wedding. She names her own habit of waiting for proof as her main risk. Her plans stay grounded in the café and home life.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd go from camp to the café with no plan and no time to learn the business. What would help is the company giving people like me a clear timetable, and some kind of grant for small businesses so the café could survive the first rough years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it's like to be a woman out here. It's better than it was, but there's still stuff. If robots take the trucks, the camps get smaller and a lot of that goes too, which I didn't expect to think was a good thing until just now.

headlineQuote: If robots take the trucks, the camps get smaller and a lot of that goes too, which I didn't expect to think was a good thing until just now.
portrait: Maya Moreau is a 27-year-old water cart driver and trainee excavator operator who flies in and out to a large gold mine, two weeks on and one week home. Her partner Luca runs a café in the city, and they have about a year of costs saved, partly with an eye on a second café. She uses AI now and then and waits for proof before changing course. In the steady and slower AGI pictures she sees automation as a way to work from the city and be home; in the two-year picture she would fall back on the café, anxious but glad to be home.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she would go straight from the mine camp to the café with no plan and no time to learn the business.
whatWouldHelp: A clear timetable from the company and grants for small businesses so the café could survive the first rough years.
